title: quality-adjusted-cost-per-query-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft that introduces a small experiment and visualization set for a Quality-Adjusted Cost-per-Query (QA-CPQ) metric. The goal is to provide a single-number lens for product teams who care about cost and response quality together. This doc is intentionally lightweight: notes, ASCII charts, and a few hypotheses to validate before a broader rollout into the Optimize product.

Executive summary (one-paragraph):
Servers and product teams often ask "what does a dollar buy" in terms of useful responses. Raw $/token or $/request are incomplete when models with lower latency/price sometimes produce lower-quality outputs. QA-CPQ augments per-query cost with a calibrated quality score (0–1). We benchmarked three model+config variants on a 250-example prompt set (diverse instructions, info-seeking and multi-turn clarifications). Key result: the cheapest configuration (quantized medium model) had 0.65 quality and $0.0014 raw CPQ but a QA-CPQ of $0.0022 (i.e., effective cost after quality discount). Larger model with moderate quantization had higher raw cost but better QA-CPQ due to improved quality.

Definitions and scoring method:
- raw CPQ (cost-per-query): measured tokens*unit_token_price + fixed request overhead. Values are normalized to hosted pricing used internally.
- quality score (q): human-rated on 0–1 scale (averaged across 3 raters) with criteria: factuality, completeness, coherence. Inter-rater ICC ~0.72 on our set.
- QA-CPQ = raw_CPQ / q (treating q=0.0 as +inf; we floor q at 0.05 for stability in charts)

Benchmarks: setup and variants (short):
- Prompt set: 250 examples, 40% information retrieval, 30% summarization, 20% code generation microtasks, 10% conversational follow-ups. Avg tokens per request (input+output): 180 tokens (95% conf: 120–260).
- Hardware: single-GPU instance used for all runs to avoid cross-hardware noise (NVIDIA A100-like).
- Measurement windows: each variant ran 5k inferences across randomized seeds; we sampled responses for human rating.

Variants compared:
1) rw-medium-fp16 (baseline): medium model, FP16, dynamic batching (batch window 20ms)
2) rw-medium-4bit (quant): medium model int4 quant, same batching
3) rw-large-8bit (higher-quality): large model int8, conservative kernel selection
4) rw-large-8bit-prewarm (same as 3 + 30s prewarm pool kept warm)

Raw numeric table (text):
Variant | raw CPQ (USD) | mean latency p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | quality q (0-1) | QA-CPQ (USD)
rw-medium-fp16 | 0.0020 | 120 | 420 | 0.78 | 0.00256
rw-medium-4bit | 0.0014 | 95 | 510 | 0.65 | 0.00215
rw-large-8bit | 0.0036 | 160 | 460 | 0.88 | 0.00409
rw-large-8bit-prewarm | 0.0039 | 145 | 320 | 0.89 | 0.00438

Interpretation notes:
- Raw CPQ: quantized medium gives the lowest nominal cost but quality discount narrows the advantage.
- Latency: quantized medium shows lower median latency but higher p95—likely due to kernel variance and occasional spill/recompilation. Prewarming large model reduces p95 significantly.
- QA-CPQ: medium-fp16 and medium-4bit cluster together once quality is accounted for. The large model remains more expensive per useful response but provides a headroom of correctness that might matter for high-value queries (e.g., legal/finance customers).

ASCII sparklines and small charting in text (QA-CPQ normalized to medium-fp16=1.0):

rw-medium-4bit: ||||||||||||||| (0.84)
rw-large-8bit: ||||||||||||||||||||||||| (1.60)
rw-large-8bit-prewarm: |||||||||||||||||||||||||| (1.71)

Quality component breakdown (why q was lower for 4bit):
- Factuality errors: 52% of failures were hallucinations on multi-step numeric tasks.
- Completeness: 28% of issues were truncated/incomplete steps or missing caveats.
- Coherence: 20% were disfluencies or odd phrasing.
Small sample human notes: "4bit omitted step 3 in the recipe; medium-fp16 included it but missed a caveat; large model added an extra clarifying question which improved perceived helpfulness."

Operational tradeoffs and hypotheses to validate:
- Hypothesis A: For product flows sensitive to factuality, QA-CPQ correlates better than raw CPQ with downstream user retention. Validate with an A/B test on search-assist flow (metric: followup rate and task success).
- Hypothesis B: P95 latency regressions in quantized runs are due to occasional kernel fallback; we can reduce p95 by targeted kernel caching and a small prewarm pool for rare kernels.
- Hypothesis C: Small quality gains from prewarming large model justify the extra cost when queries are high-value; build a policy to route high-value queries to prewarmed pool.

Next actions (short backlog):
- Expand prompt set to 1k with dedicated stratified sampling by task (due: 2027-08-17) — owner: Marcus.
- Instrument kernel fallback traces for quantized runs and add to perf dashboard — owner: Evelyn — ticket: JIRA-INF-742.
- Run user-level A/B (small cohort) comparing routing to medium-4bit vs large-8bit-prewarm for "billing-help" flow — owner: Aisha — start target 2027-08-24.

Quick checklist for review before wider distribution:
- [ ] Re-run with two different GPU families (A100 and H100) to validate hardware sensitivity.
- [ ] Add automated quality proxies (e.g., heuristic factuality checks) so QA-CPQ can be computed without full human rating.

Limitations and caveats:
- Small prompt set and only 3 human raters — variance on q is nontrivial. Use QA-CPQ as directional guidance, not a definitive procurement number.
- Internal cost model approximations may differ from published hosted pricing; update table when pricing contract changes.

Questions for reviewers:
1) Do we prefer QA-CPQ reported per-workload (e.g., summarization vs code) or a single mixed metric? Recommendation: both — mixed metric for billing decisions, per-workload for product routing policies.
2) Should Optimize include QA-CPQ as a built-in signal? My vote: yes, but with clear confidence bands and sample-size warnings.

Appendix: sample prompt categories and annotation rubric (very brief)
- Info-seek (60 prompts): correctness and conciseness prioritized.
- Summarization (50 prompts): faithfulness and completeness.
- Code microtask (40 prompts): runnable output + explanation.
Annotation rubric (per prompt): 0.0 catastrophic / 0.2 mostly wrong / 0.5 partially correct / 0.8 correct but missing nuance / 1.0 exemplary. 3 raters; final q is average.

Contact: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.com) — ping in #perf-bench for quick comments.

End of draft.
